Alle alle.note: The little auk, nesting by the million in High Arctic scree and wintering on the open North Atlantic.

Aptenodytes patagonicus.note: The king penguin, breeding in colonies of hundreds of thousands on the subantarctic islands.

Architeuthis.note: The giant squid, reaching twelve metres and known for most of history only from carcasses and sperm-whale scars.

Avicennia marina.note: The grey mangrove, the most salt- and cold-tolerant of all, fringing desert coasts from the Red Sea to New Zealand.

Carcharodon carcharias.note: The great white shark, descended from broad-toothed makos about six million years ago.

Ceratioidei.note: Deep-sea anglerfishes, luring prey with a glowing bait; in some, the dwarf male fuses to the female for life.
Ceratioidei.conf_note: oldest body fossils Miocene; molecular dates put the split near the Oligocene

Chaetodontidae.note: Butterflyfishes, coral-pickers whose numbers rise and fall with the reef itself.

Cheloniidae.note: Hard-shelled sea turtles: green, hawksbill, loggerhead and their Cretaceous forerunners.

Delphinidae.note: Oceanic dolphins, from spinners to orcas; a late-Miocene radiation that now fills every sea.

Dermochelys coriacea.note: The leatherback, a half-tonne turtle that follows jellyfish from the tropics to subpolar water.

Diomedea exulans.note: The wandering albatross, with the widest wingspan of any living bird, circling the Southern Ocean between breeding seasons.

Diomedeidae.note: Albatrosses, gliding the wind belts for years between landfalls on remote islands.

Dosidicus gigas.note: The Humboldt or jumbo squid, hunting in shoals of thousands along the eastern Pacific.

Dugong dugon.note: The dugong, the one strictly marine sea cow left, grazing seagrass from the Red Sea to the Coral Sea.

Exocoetidae.note: Flying fishes, gliding tens of metres on enlarged fins to escape tuna and dolphinfish.

Fulmarus glacialis.note: The northern fulmar, a cold-water petrel that nests on sea cliffs from Brittany to the High Arctic.

Halophila stipulacea.note: A small seagrass of the Red Sea and western Indian Ocean, growing from the shallows to fifty metres down.

Hexanchus.note: Sixgill sharks, a lineage little changed since the Jurassic, cruising the dark continental slopes.

Istiophoridae.note: Marlins and sailfish, the fastest fishes of the open tropical ocean.

Isurus.note: Mako sharks, the fastest of all sharks and ocean-wide hunters of tuna and swordfish.

Lophelia pertusa.note: A cold-water coral building reefs in the dark, hundreds of metres down, along continental slopes and seamounts.

Macrouridae.note: Grenadiers or rattails, the commonest fishes of the continental slope and the abyssal plain.

Mirounga leonina.note: The southern elephant seal, bulls of four tonnes hauling out on subantarctic beaches to fight and breed.

Mobula.note: Manta and devil rays, filter-feeders that leap clear of the water in schools of thousands.

Myctophidae.note: Lanternfishes, perhaps the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, rising hundreds of metres to the surface every night.

Octocorallia.note: Soft corals, sea fans and bamboo corals; on seamounts they form forests that can be thousands of years old.

Onychoprion fuscatus.note: The sooty tern, which stays on the wing for years at sea and breeds in vast colonies on tropical islets.

Osedax.note: Bone-eating worms that bore into whale skeletons on the sea floor; their traces go back to plesiosaur bones.
Osedax.conf_note: Osedax borings are known from Cretaceous plesiosaur and turtle bone; the PBDB dates only the named traces

Otariidae.note: Sea lions and fur seals, a North Pacific family that crossed the equator about six million years ago.

Phaethon.note: Tropicbirds, plunge-divers of the warm open ocean that nest on the remotest islands.
Phaethon.conf_note: the genus has almost no fossil record; tropicbirds (Prophaethon) are Eocene

Phocidae.note: True seals, which arose in the North Atlantic and reached the Antarctic pack ice by the late Miocene.

Phocoena sinus.note: The vaquita, the smallest and rarest cetacean, confined to the turbid head of the Gulf of California.

Physalia physalis.note: The Portuguese man o' war, a colony of specialised animals sailing under a gas-filled float.

Physeter macrocephalus.note: The sperm whale, the largest toothed predator alive, diving past two kilometres to hunt squid in the dark.

Physeteroidea.note: Sperm whales in their Miocene variety, from dwarf forms to Livyatan, a raptorial hunter of other whales.

Procellariiformes.note: Petrels, shearwaters and storm-petrels: tube-nosed seabirds that come ashore only to breed.

Prochlorococcus.note: The smallest and most numerous photosynthesiser known, making a large share of the oxygen produced by the open ocean.

Pyrosoma.note: Pyrosomes: glowing colonial tunicates, hollow tubes that can grow longer than a whale.

Rhincodon typus.note: The whale shark, the largest fish alive, filtering plankton at the surface of warm seas.

Sargassum.note: Sargassum weeds, attached on warm rocky shores and, in two Atlantic species, drifting free in mid-ocean.

Sargassum natans.note: Free-floating sargassum, the golden weed of the Sargasso Sea, carrying its own community of fish, crabs and turtles.

Somniosus microcephalus.note: The Greenland shark, the longest-lived vertebrate known; individuals are thought to reach four centuries.
Somniosus microcephalus.conf_note: extant; the PBDB holds only Pliocene teeth

Spheniscidae.note: Penguins, flightless divers since the Paleocene; several Eocene and Oligocene species stood as tall as a person.

Stylophora pistillata.note: A branching reef coral of the Indo-Pacific; its Red Sea populations tolerate unusually hot water.

Thalassia testudinum.note: Turtle grass, forming the great seagrass meadows of the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.

Thalassodendron ciliatum.note: The seagrass of Saya de Malha, a drowned bank in mid-ocean carrying the largest seagrass meadow on Earth.

Thunnus.note: Tunas: warm-blooded, ocean-crossing predators built for sustained speed.

Totoaba macdonaldi.note: The totoaba, a two-metre drum found only in the Gulf of California, spawning at the Colorado River's mouth.

Trichodesmium erythraeum.note: 'Sea sawdust', a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium whose rust-coloured blooms streak warm, nutrient-poor seas.

Vampyroteuthis infernalis.note: The vampire squid, last of an order older than the dinosaurs, drifting in the oxygen-minimum zone on marine snow.

Xenophyophorea.note: Giant single-celled organisms of the abyssal plain, some the size of a fist, building shells from sediment.

Zalophus californianus.note: The California sea lion, breeding on the desert islands of the Gulf of California and the Pacific coast.

Ziphiidae.note: Beaked whales, the deepest-diving mammals: Cuvier's beaked whale has been logged at nearly three kilometres.

Zostera marina.note: Eelgrass, the seagrass of cool northern shores, nursery to cod, scallops and brent geese.
